frame.objective: Determine whether Neumann should create a differentiated product proposition for home-studio creators and other individual buyers beyond its current professional studio offering, or maintain a single professional range for all customers, based on evidence of market demand, current individual buyer reach, and potential value capture.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Must consider at least three strategic alternatives, including no expansion.
Evidence must address demand, current individual buyer reach, and value capture mechanisms.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated proposition for home-studio creators and individual buyers (new products/features tailored to their needs).
2) Keep one professional range for everyone (no differentiation, same products for all customers).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional studio market without new offerings.

T1.claim: Home-studio creators and individual buyers will increase purchase of Neumann products if offered a differentiated proposition that addresses their specific needs (e.g., affordable entry-level mics, tailored tutorials, or studio-in-a-box kits).
T1.who_benefits: Neumann gains higher volume sales and premium pricing by appealing to a broader segment.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Creators shift from budget brands to Neumann when they perceive a clear value proposition that meets their workflow and quality expectations.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Neumann can capture value through expanded product lines, subscription services, and bundled kits, leveraging its existing brand prestige and academy content to differentiate from competitors.
assumptions: Creators currently avoid Neumann due to perceived high price or lack of entry-level options.
A differentiated proposition will be adopted if it offers tangible benefits (e.g., lower price, specific features, or integrated learning).
The market is large enough to support additional volume without cannibalizing professional sales.
predictions: If offered a differentiated proposition, purchase intent among creators will increase by at least 15% compared to the current baseline.
Sales of entry-level Neumann products will grow faster than overall professional sales in the next 12 months.
Creator satisfaction scores will rise, leading to positive word-of-mouth and repeat purchases.
T1.first_claim: Home-studio creators and individual buyers will increase purchase of Neumann products if offered a differentiated proposition that addresses their specific needs (e.g., affordable entry-level mics, tailored tutorials, or studio-in-a-box kits).

T2.claim: Home-studio creators will increase purchase of Neumann products if they perceive that the brand offers a premium, trusted audio experience that signals professional credibility, leading them to choose Neumann over competitors even at higher prices.
T2.who_benefits: Neumann gains premium pricing and brand equity by being the choice of professionals.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Creators associate Neumann with high quality and status, so they are willing to pay more for perceived authority in their work.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Neumann can capture value through premium pricing, limited editions, and brand licensing, leveraging its existing professional reputation to justify higher costs.
assumptions: Creators value brand prestige as a signal of quality and professionalism.
They are willing to pay a premium for products associated with professionals.
The Neumann brand is currently perceived as professional rather than consumer.
predictions: If a survey shows that creators rank Neumann highest for perceived professional credibility, purchase intent will increase by at least 15% compared to a generic brand.
Willingness to pay a premium (e.g., 20% above competitor price) will be observed in a controlled test.
Creators will cite brand reputation as a primary reason for choosing Neumann over budget alternatives.

assumptions: Boat owners in target markets (e.g., Scandinavia, Europe) have discretionary spending for boat aesthetics.
Jotun can produce a differentiated, visible finish that differentiates it from competitors.
A direct-to-consumer channel can be established at acceptable cost.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available up to 1993.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, weight management, or medical self‑monitoring).

Time‑saving is a primary driver for purchase decisions.
Tanita’s existing scale brand is trusted by professionals for accuracy.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (Test X1) before any further investment. The evidence base is limited to company claims about medical necessity and household adoption, which do not directly prove consumer demand or willingness to pay. Until real consumer data is available, any decision would be speculative.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available up to 1993.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about Tanita’s current reach to individual buyers; must be discovered.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, weight management, or medical self‑monitoring).
2) Expand the existing B2B offering to additional health clubs or clinics without creating a consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on commercial scales and existing professional customers.
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to third parties for consumer applications.

T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can charge premium prices for a consumer version, leveraging its existing brand trust and medical credibility to justify higher costs.

Tanita’s household scale dominance signals quality and trust.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 1.5 times the price of standard consumer scales for a health‑focused model.
Purchase intent will be higher among respondents who report regular doctor consultations for health monitoring.

X1.name: Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Health-Focused Bioelectrical Impedance Scale
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are recruited from a Japanese panel to match the household demographic profile. They are shown a description of a stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser positioned as a medical-grade home health tool. They are asked: "Would you purchase this device at a price of ¥15,000 (approx. €120 in 1993) for home use?" (Yes/No).
X1.sample: 300 respondents, balanced by age and gender to match the Japanese household demographic.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness-to-pay (binary). Secondary measure: self-reported health concern (e.g., BMI tracking, weight loss goal).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent ≥50% among respondents who report health concern; willingness-to-pay ≥50%.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent ≥50% among respondents who report personal health goal; willingness-to-pay ≥50%.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent among health-concern group ≥50% AND willingness-to-pay among health-concern group ≥50%, proceed to develop a health-focused consumer proposition. If purchase intent among personal-goal group ≥50% AND willingness-to-pay among personal-goal group ≥50%,

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (Test X1) before any further investment. The evidence base is limited to company claims about medical necessity and household adoption, which do not directly prove consumer demand or willingness to pay. Until real consumer data is available, any decision would be speculative.
final.target_customer: Japanese households with health concerns seeking accurate body-fat measurements for personal health monitoring.
final.value_proposition: A premium-priced, medical-grade stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser positioned as a home health tool that leverages Tanita’s existing brand trust and medical credibility.
final.next_action: Run Test X1 (Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Survey) with 300 respondents to measure purchase intent and willingness-to-pay among health-concern respondents.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 (medical necessity) and T2 (personal health goal) remain uncertain due to lack of direct consumer demand evidence. The survey will clarify which mechanism drives willingness to pay.
would_change_if: If the survey shows purchase intent ≥50% among health-concern respondents and willingness-to-pay ≥50%, proceed to develop a health-focused consumer proposition. If personal-goal respondents show similar results, reconsider the proposition.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Medical Necessity vs Personal Health Goal
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants view a product description of a stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser and are asked about their primary reason for purchase (medical necessity vs personal health goal). They then indicate willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale. The test also collects demographic data (age, gender, BMI).
X1.sample: 500 Japanese adults recruited via an online panel, balanced for age and gender, stratified by BMI (normal, overweight, obese).
X1.measure: Primary reason for purchase (medical vs personal) and average WTP (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 60% of participants will cite medical necessity as primary reason, and average WTP will be above €120 (reflecting premium price).
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 60% will cite personal health goal as primary reason, and average WTP will be below €120.

X1.decision_rule: If ≥60% cite medical necessity AND average WTP ≥€120 → evidence supports T1. If ≥60% cite personal health goal AND average WTP <€120 → evidence supports T2. If neither condition is met → insufficient evidence for either theory.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, household adoption, or willingness to pay for a consumer bioelectrical impedance scale. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct a low‑cost test (e.g., the proposed Consumer Preference Test) to gather direct evidence of consumer demand before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Health‑conscious households in Japan who already track body composition using existing household scales.
final.value_proposition: A premium‑priced, medically‑backed stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyser that leverages Tanita’s household scale reputation to capture consumer market share.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (or a simpler survey) within the €15,000 budget and 12‑week timeline to measure purchase motivation and willingness to pay.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 (medical necessity) and T2 (personal health goal) remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence from 1993 sources.
would_change_if: If the test shows ≥60% of participants cite medical necessity and average willingness to pay ≥€120, T1 would become likely and investment could proceed.
If the test shows ≥60% cite personal health goal and average willingness to pay <€120, T2 would become likely and a different value proposition would be considered.
If the test shows neither condition met, both theories would remain uncertain and further testing would be needed.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Medical Necessity vs Personal Health Goal
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants view a product description of a stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser and are asked about their primary reason for purchase (medical necessity vs personal health goal). They then indicate willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale. The test also collects demographic data (age, gender, BMI).
arguments.sample: 500 Japanese adults recruited via an online panel, balanced for age and gender, stratified by BMI (normal, overweight, obese).
arguments.measure: Primary reason for purchase (medical vs personal) and average WTP (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 60% of participants will cite medical necessity as primary reason, and average WTP will be above €120 (reflecting premium price).
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 60% will cite personal health goal as primary reason, and average WTP will be below €120.

arguments.decision_rule: If ≥60% cite medical necessity AND average WTP ≥€120 → evidence supports T1. If ≥60% cite personal health goal AND average WTP <€120 → evidence supports T2. If neither condition is met → insufficient evidence for either theory.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct a low‑cost test (e.g., the proposed Consumer Preference Test) to gather direct evidence of consumer demand before committing resources.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available up to 1993.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about Tanita’s current reach to individual buyers; must be discovered.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, weight management, or medical self‑monitoring).
2) Expand the existing B2B offering to additional health clubs or clinics without creating a consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on commercial scales and existing professional customers.
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to third parties for consumer applications.

T1.claim: Health‑conscious consumers will adopt a stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyser for home use because they view it as a convenient, accurate way to monitor body composition for weight management and health.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers seeking to track body fat and maintain health.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing public awareness of health risks linked to excess body fat (as shown by medical evidence and media coverage) makes accurate, non‑invasive measurement desirable.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can charge a premium for a consumer‑friendly product, sell through retail channels, and leverage its existing household scale brand to command higher margins.
assumptions: Consumers trust medical evidence linking body fat to health risks.
Tanita’s existing scale brand is trusted by Japanese households.
A stand‑on device is perceived as easier and faster than traditional scales.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 10% above a comparable commercial scale for home body‑fat analysis.
Pilot sales in a test market will show a conversion rate of at least 5% of interested consumers purchasing the device within 12 weeks.
Repeat purchases for additional family members will occur at a rate of at least 30% within 24 weeks.
T1.first_claim: Health‑conscious consumers will adopt a stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyser for home use because they view it as a convenient, accurate way to monitor body composition for weight management and health.

T2.claim: Health clubs and clinics will adopt the stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyser because it provides a fast, non‑invasive way to assess client body composition, enabling personalized fitness programs and improving client retention.
T2.who_benefits: Fitness professionals and health club operators seeking to enhance service quality and member engagement.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Professionals need data that is quick, reliable, and actionable to design personalized training plans; the analyser offers a competitive advantage over competitors who lack such tools.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can sell the device at a premium to commercial scales, bundle it with membership packages, and offer data management services, generating recurring revenue from service contracts.
assumptions: Fitness professionals value data that directly influences training design.
Time‑saving is a primary driver for purchase decisions.
Tanita’s existing scale brand is trusted by professionals for accuracy.
predictions: Health clubs will place orders for at least 20 units within 12 weeks of a demo, indicating a conversion rate of 10% of interested providers.
Contract renewals will include a 20% increase in membership fees for access to the analyser, generating recurring revenue.
Competitor adoption of similar devices will be observed within 18 months, leading to a price premium of at least 15% for Tanita.
T2.first_claim: Health clubs and clinics will adopt the stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyser because it provides a fast, non‑invasive way to assess client body composition, enabling personalized fitness programs and improving client retention.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available up to 1993.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about Tanita’s current reach to individual buyers; must be discovered.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, weight management, or medical self‑monitoring).
2) Expand the existing B2B offering to additional health clubs or clinics without creating a consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on commercial scales and existing professional customers.
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to third parties for consumer applications.

T1.claim: Health‑conscious consumers will purchase a stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyser for home use because they view it as a medical necessity that provides actionable health insights.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Increased public awareness of body‑fat links to chronic diseases (as indicated by medical evidence) and the availability of a convenient, non‑invasive home device.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can charge premium prices for a medical‑grade device and sell directly to consumers, capturing higher margins than bulk B2B sales.
assumptions: Consumers trust medical evidence linking body fat to health risks.
Home use is feasible and convenient for regular tracking.
Tanita’s brand is associated with medical accuracy due to its professional market presence.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 1.5x the price of standard consumer scales for a body‑fat analyser.
Purchase intent will be higher among those who report regular health monitoring or weight‑tracking habits.
Sales of the home device will correlate with regions where obesity rates are higher and health awareness is promoted.

X1.name: Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Home Bioelectrical Impedance Body-Fat Analyzer
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two price points (premium vs standard). They indicate purchase intent and willingness to pay. The test measures whether premium pricing (aligned with medical necessity) drives higher intent than standard pricing (aligned with status signaling).
X1.sample: 500 Japanese adults aged 25-55, recruited via an online panel to match regional demographics. Stratify by gender and income to ensure diversity.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy at this price") and willingness-to-pay (EUR amount). Secondary: self-reported motivation (open-ended).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium price group will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than standard price group.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Standard price group will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than premium price group.

final.target_customer: Health‑conscious consumers in Japan who already own bathroom scales and are interested in tracking body composition for personal health management.
final.value_proposition: A stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyzer marketed as a medical‑grade home device that provides actionable health insights, sold at a premium price to reflect professional accuracy and medical necessity.
final.next_action: Execute Test X1 (Consumer Willingness‑to‑Pay Survey) within the 12‑week timeline and €15,000 budget, using the specified sample, method, and decision rule.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 (health‑necessity motivation) and T2 (status‑signaling motivation) remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence from 1993 sources. The survey will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the survey shows premium pricing yields at least a 15% higher willingness‑to‑pay than standard pricing, proceed with the health‑necessity proposition. If standard pricing yields a higher premium, reconsider the status‑driven approach.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available as of late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.
constraints: Limited to public sources published on or before late 2002; no internal company data.
Investment justification must be based on evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, or competitive advantage.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Evidence must address the specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness, remote work) and the technology's suitability for it.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/industrial focus without targeting individual consumers (status quo).
3) Pursue a different route to market or customer group (e.g., partnering with outdoor retailers, offering a subscription service) while retaining the core technology.
4) No expansion: continue focusing on current markets and product lines.

constraints: Limited to public sources published on or before late 2002; no internal company data.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/industrial focus without targeting individual consumers (status quo).
3) Pursue a different route to market or customer group (e.g., partnering with outdoor retailers, offering a subscription service) while retaining the core technology.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available as of late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.
constraints: Limited to public sources published on or before late 2002; no internal company data.
Investment justification must be based on evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, or competitive advantage.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Evidence must address the specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness, remote work) and the technology's suitability for it.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/industrial focus without targeting individual consumers (status quo).
3) Pursue a different route to market or customer group (e.g., partnering with outdoor retailers, offering a subscription service) while retaining the core technology.
4) No expansion: continue focusing on current markets and product lines.

T1.who_benefits: Consumers who engage in high‑risk outdoor activities (e.g., hikers, climbers, remote workers) benefit from a device that can summon help in case of distress.

T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can capture value by selling the beacons directly to consumers through retail channels (outdoor gear stores, online) at a premium price, leveraging the technology’s safety reputation.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation market in the U.S. is large and growing in 2002.
Consumers are aware of the existence of 406 MHz distress beacons and understand their functionality.
Price sensitivity is moderate; a device that saves lives is valued even at a higher cost.
predictions: If offered in outdoor retail, at least 10% of surveyed hikers/climbers would express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Sales would be concentrated in regions with high outdoor activity density (e.g., national parks).

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available as of late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.
constraints: Limited to public sources published on or before late 2002; no internal company data.
Investment justification must be based on evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, or competitive advantage.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Evidence must address the specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness, remote work) and the technology's suitability for it.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/industrial focus without targeting individual consumers (status quo).
3) Pursue a different route to market or customer group (e.g., partnering with outdoor retailers, offering a subscription service) while retaining the core technology.
4) No expansion: continue focusing on current markets and product lines.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available as of late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.
constraints: Limited to public sources published on or before late 2002; no internal company data.
Investment justification must be based on evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, or competitive advantage.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Evidence must address the specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness, remote work) and the technology's suitability for it.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/industrial focus without targeting individual consumers (status quo).
3) Pursue a different route to market or customer group (e.g., partnering with outdoor retailers, offering a subscription service) while retaining the core technology.
4) No expansion: continue focusing on current markets and product lines.

T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can capture value by selling the beacons directly to consumers through retail channels (outdoor gear stores, online) at a premium price, leveraging the technology’s safety reputation.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation market in the U.S. is large and growing in 2002.
Consumers are aware of the existence of 406 MHz distress beacons and understand their functionality.
Price sensitivity is moderate; a device that saves lives is valued even at a higher cost.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available as of mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, or competitive advantage.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Alternatives must include no expansion, a different route to buyers, a different customer group, and a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑holder farming, hobby gardening, or a niche agricultural activity) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers directly without creating a differentiated consumer proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current B2B dealer model and existing product lines.
4) Target a different customer group (e.g., urban gardeners, small‑scale commercial growers) with a modified product or service.
5) Pursue a different route to market (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer sales, mail‑order, or partnerships) while keeping the core tractor business unchanged.
